# The question, and the one-paragraph answer

**IB1** is a composite lymph node from one patient: classic Hodgkin lymphoma together with
follicular lymphoma. Steps 07–13 localised both lesions inside it and concluded there is
**"no spatial relationship between the two diseases"**. That is a headline claim about the
one thing a composite node is uniquely able to answer, and it rested on a single test.
Step 17 later named the design that would settle the question properly — *"a within-IB1
design comparing FL tissue near and far from the Hodgkin field, which needs no cross-sample
subtraction"* — and it had not been run. **This step is that design.**

It matters that the design is within-IB1. Every cross-sample route is closed: the
IB1-vs-RB1 FL contrast is not identifiable (2 of 89 bins find a composition-matched
partner), and for the exhaustion and chemokine genes the between-slide offset exceeds every
within-slide regional effect. A contrast computed inside one sample, one section and one
cell type at a time carries no slide term, no composition term and nothing to subtract.

```{r headline, results="asis"}
if (!is.null(GV) && !is.null(AV)) {
  n_h1 <- if (is.null(h1)) NA else nrow(h1)
  cat(sprintf('
<div class="verdict-mid">
**Three results, and the first one is a method correction.**

**The intuitive axis does not work, and finding that out was the point of running a gate
first.** Distance from FL tissue to the nearest Hodgkin hotspot *looks* like the exposure
axis and is what step 12 used. It fails its own positive control: CCL17+CCL22 inside FL
tissue is **%.1f cp10k in the near half against %.1f in the far half** — the wrong way round —
and field exposure is uncorrelated with distance-to-hotspot across the FL fields of view
(rho = **%.3f**, *p* = %.2f). The cause is that the hotspots are the top 1%% of chemokine
bins and do not enumerate the field\'s sources, which step 17 had already flagged. The axis
that works is each bin\'s **own** local field level, which spans **%.0fx** across the FL
fields of view.

**The arrangement of the two lesions is UNRESOLVED, and step 13\'s clean null does not
survive scrutiny even though its verdict does.** Against a null that relocates the Hodgkin
foci at random while preserving their number, sizes and internal clustering, the observed
hotspot-to-FL distance of **%d um** sits against a null median of **%d um**
(*p* = **%.2f**). But the real hotspots sit in more over-fixation-depleted, more peripheral
tissue than average, and defect burden rises with distance to the FL foci -- so a uniform
null relocates them into tissue intrinsically closer to the FL. Matching the null on defect
burden moves the null median to **%s um** and the two directions to *p* = **%s** and
**%s**. Nothing reaches significance either way, so step 13\'s verdict stands; the claim
that it is a *clean* null does not.

**Inside FL tissue, the field response is not distinguishable from ordinary IB1 tissue --
in expression or in composition.** Of 44 pre-declared genes tested in each of three cell
```

# What is being replaced

<div class="verdict-no">
**Step 13's claim rests entirely on one test in step 12**, and it has three defects that all
push toward a null that was never really tested.

`output/12_fl_vs_hodgkin/IB1_fl_vs_hodgkin_distance_postqc.csv` holds the whole of it: the
distance from each Hodgkin hotspot bin to the nearest FL-like focus (median 1,035 um)
against the same distance for non-hotspot bins (1,205 um), Wilcoxon *p* = 0.233, on
**11 FL foci**. Note the direction — the hotspots were nominally *closer*.

1. **The unit is the bin.** Bins inside one field of view are not independent, and both
   lesions are spatially clustered.
2. **The comparison set is unmatched.** A bin can only *be* a hotspot if it carries enough
   cells for a stable cp10k, so "non-hotspot bins" have a different propensity to be
   labelled at all.
3. **Tissue geometry is ignored.** Both lesions can only occur where tissue is, and IB1 is
   in three pieces.
</div>

<div class="verdict-mid">
**One of those three turns out not to matter, and saying so is part of the correction.**
Recomputing step 12's own statistic with the **field of view** as the unit — pairing each
FOV's hotspot bins against its own other bins — gives
*p* = **`r g("step12_fov_paired_p", AV)`** against the published
**`r g("step12_bin_p_reported", AV)`**. The unit choice was *not* what produced that null;
it was null either way. The defects that mattered were the unmatched reference and the
absence of a geometry-preserving null.
</div>

# Axis selection, which is a result in its own right

Nothing was contrasted until an axis had passed a gate. The project has already lost a
design to non-identifiability discovered *after* the contrast was computed — step 16's C3
and C4, where 2 of 89 FL bins found a composition-matched partner and the
difference-in-differences meant to rescue it was withdrawn. So the question here was asked
in the other order: does a contrast exist, and on what axis?

```{r axis-fig}
img(file.path(IF, "figures/fig_21_axis_selection.png"))
```

```{r axis-tables}
kb(AA[, .(variable, near = hi, far = lo, smd, p_wilcox, flag)],
   caption = "AXIS A (distance to hotspot): balance of the near/far strata, FOV means")
kb(BA[, .(variable, high = hi, low = lo, smd, p_wilcox, flag)],
   caption = "AXIS B (own field level): balance of the low/high strata, FOV means")
```

<div class="verdict-no">
**AXIS A — distance to the nearest hotspot — is REJECTED.** It passes the geometric part of
the gate: the `r g("fl_bins")` FL bins in `r g("fl_fovs")` fields of view split into
`r g("fovs_near", GV)`/`r g("fovs_far", GV)` arms whose median distances differ by
**`r g("axisA_sep_um")` um**, more than one field length. It fails the part that matters.
The chemokines that *define* the field are **`r g("axisA_chemo_near")` cp10k** in the near
arm and **`r g("axisA_chemo_far")`** in the far arm, and across the FL fields of view
exposure and distance are uncorrelated (rho = `r g("axisA_rho_exposure_vs_dist")`,
*p* = `r g("axisA_p")`). An axis that does not order the thing it is supposed to measure
cannot carry a contrast.

**Why it fails, and it is not the tissue pieces.** Two candidate causes were separable and
were separated. Cross-piece Euclidean distance — which is not a diffusion path — turns out
to affect **0%** of FL bins, so that is not it. What is left is the source set: the hotspots
are IB1's top 1% of chemokine bins, and only **`r g("hotspot_bins")` of the 80** survive the
low-information filter. Step 17 had already written down that distance-to-peak is *"blind by
construction, since the peaks are only the top 1% of chemokine bins, not all HRS
locations"*. FL fields of view 693 and 694 make it concrete: ~3,000 um from any hotspot,
carrying 37 and 77 cp10k.
</div>

<div class="verdict-ok">
**AXIS B — each bin's own field level — is USABLE**, and is the axis
`16_script_field_gradient.R` already used successfully for eight pre-declared genes. Across
the FL fields of view it spans **`r g("axisB_spread_fold")`x**, from below IB1's field cut
(11.4 cp10k) to well above it without reaching the hotspot cut (176.1). The split is at the
FL fields' own median, so the arms are balanced in count by construction and the threshold
is not tuned to any outcome.
</div>

<div class="verdict-mid">
**One imbalance shapes the whole downstream design.** On axis B, field exposure and B-cell
share are collinear inside FL tissue — `fb_a` SMD **`r g("axisB_fb_a_smd")`**. This is not
news: `CLAUDE.md` fact 4 already records that IB1's B-dense tissue is where the Hodgkin
chemokines concentrate. The consequence is that **cell-type conditioning is mandatory here,
not a refinement**. A bin-level contrast on this axis would re-measure B share, which is
exactly how step 16's C3 contrast failed — it returned RB1's interfollicular markers as
"up in IB1 FL".
</div>

```{r pieces}
kb(PZ, caption = "IB1's tissue pieces. Piece 4 carries hotspots and no FL; distances across the gaps between pieces are not diffusion paths.")
```

# Are the two lesions arranged dependently?

```{r arr-fig}
img(file.path(IF, "figures/fig_21_arrangement.png"))
```

Two statistics, both directions, with the tissue mask held fixed by construction, against
two nulls that fail in opposite ways.

<div class="verdict-no">
**This result is BRACKETED, not settled, and the over-fixation defect is why.** Two
defensible nulls give different answers, and the difference is not noise — it is the rim
geometry of the defect. Read both before drawing a conclusion.
</div>

<div class="verdict-mid">
**NULL R — uniform focus relocation — is null.** The
`r g("n_hotspots", AV)` hotspot bins form `r g("nullR_foci", AV)` connected foci; each focus
keeps its size and internal shape and is re-sited at a random occupied bin.
Hotspot-to-nearest-FL is **`r g("obs_h2f_um", AV)` um** observed against a null median of
`r g("nullR_h2f_med", AV)` um, 95% interval
[`r g("nullR_h2f_lo", AV)`, `r g("nullR_h2f_hi", AV)`], ***p* = `r g("nullR_h2f_p", AV)`**.
The reverse direction, FL-to-nearest-hotspot, gives `r g("obs_f2h_um", AV)` um against
`r g("nullR_f2h_med", AV)`, *p* = `r g("nullR_f2h_p", AV)`. Both observed values sit slightly
below the null median — the lesions are marginally closer than chance — and nowhere near
significance. **But this null sites foci uniformly over occupied tissue, and the real
hotspots do not sit in average tissue.**
</div>

<div class="verdict-no">
**NULL Rd — defect-matched relocation — moves the answer toward co-location.** Restricting
the siting pool to bins whose defect fraction falls inside the observed hotspots' own
interquartile range gives a null median of **`r g("nullRd_h2f_med", AV)` um** against the
same observed `r g("obs_h2f_um", AV)` — ***p* = `r g("nullRd_h2f_p", AV)`** — and in the
reverse direction `r g("nullRd_f2h_med", AV)` um against `r g("obs_f2h_um", AV)`,
***p* = `r g("nullRd_f2h_p", AV)`**. Neither reaches significance, but both move a long way
from NULL R's `r g("nullR_h2f_p", AV)` and `r g("nullR_f2h_p", AV)`.

**Why NULL Rd is arguably the better test of *dependence*.** The question is whether the two
lesions are arranged dependently, and each pattern's own marginal geography should therefore
be held fixed. The hotspots' marginal geography is not average: they sit in tissue with a
median defect fraction of
`r if (!is.null(DEG)) DEG[bin_region=="cHL_hotspot", med_defect] else NA` against the FL
foci's `r if (!is.null(DEG)) DEG[bin_region=="FL_focus", med_defect] else NA`, and they are
edge-biased (Wilcoxon *p* = `r g("p_hotspot_vs_bg_edge", DQ)`). And defect burden is
confounded with the outcome: it rises with distance to the nearest FL focus
(rho = **`r g("rho_defect_dist_to_fl", DQ)`**, *p* = `r g("p_defect_dist_to_fl", DQ)`),
because it is largely a rim effect (rho with distance to the tissue edge =
**`r g("rho_defect_edge", DQ)`**). So a uniform null relocates the hotspots into tissue that
is *intrinsically closer to the FL* than the tissue they actually occupy, which makes the
observed distance look ordinary.

**Why it is not simply adopted.** Defect fraction is close to a proxy for distance to the
section edge, so conditioning on it also conditions on absolute position. If the hotspots'
peripheral bias is biological rather than technical, NULL Rd removes some real signal along
with the artifact — and this data cannot separate those, which is the same wall as the
unattributed far-field residual in `CLAUDE.md` fact 3.
</div>

<div class="verdict-mid">
**What to carry forward.** Step 13's "no spatial relationship between the two diseases" is
**not overturned** — no test here reaches significance in either direction. But it is no
longer a clean null: under the null that matches the hotspots' own tissue geography the
observed distances are shorter than chance at *p* = `r g("nullRd_f2h_p", AV)`, and the
honest statement is that **the arrangement of the two lesions is unresolved at this sample
size**, with the over-fixation rim as the reason it cannot be settled rather than a nuisance
to be adjusted away. Resolving it wants more FL tissue in a section without the fixation
gradient.
</div>

<details>
<summary>A rigid rotation was tried first and is not usable on this section</summary>
The natural null is to rotate the whole hotspot pattern within the tissue mask. It gives
**0 of 5,000 admissible draws**: the primary tissue piece fills only about a third of its own
bounding box, so a 23-point pattern spanning the piece never lands back on tissue. Relocating
foci one at a time fits because each focus is a few bins across. A null with no admissible
draws is a broken null, not a negative result, and was replaced rather than reported.
</details>

<div class="verdict-no">
**NULL P — label permutation — gives a nominally significant *p* = `r g("nullP_h2f_p", AV)`,
and it is an artifact of the null.** The permutation reassigns the hotspot label among bins
matched on cell count and depth, which destroys the clustering it ought to hold fixed. That
was a prediction, and it is checkable on the drawn patterns themselves.

```{r adj}
kb(ADJ, caption = "Mean nearest-neighbour spacing WITHIN the hotspot pattern. A valid null reproduces the observed value.")
```

NULL R reproduces the observed within-pattern spacing to
**`r if (!is.null(ADJ)) round(100*ADJ$ratio_to_observed[2]) else NA`%**; NULL P inflates it
by **`r if (!is.null(ADJ)) round(100*(ADJ$ratio_to_observed[3]-1)) else NA`%**. Spreading the
hotspots out puts them farther from everything, the FL foci included, which is where the
short-looking observed value comes from. **This is the same class of error as the
pseudoreplication rule** — a statistic is only as good as the thing its null holds fixed.
</div>

<div class="verdict-mid">
**What the nulls could have detected.** The 95% interval for hotspot-to-FL under NULL R is
[`r g("nullR_h2f_lo", AV)`, `r g("nullR_h2f_hi", AV)`] um against an observed
`r g("obs_h2f_um", AV)`. So the test would have declared co-location only if the median had
fallen below about **`r g("nullR_h2f_lo", AV)` um**, a
`r if (!is.null(AV)) round(100*(1 - AV$nullR_h2f_lo/AV$nullR_h2f_med)) else NA`% reduction
against chance. Anything weaker than that is not excluded by this result.
</div>

# Does FL tissue respond to the field differently from ordinary tissue?

The primary statistic is an **interaction**, not a slope, because a gene rising with field
exposure inside FL tissue is not yet an FL-specific result: 1,723 of 6,175 genes are
field-associated tissue-wide, so the generic response has to be subtracted.

For each gene and coarse cell type: `b_fl` is the slope of expression on log2 field exposure
among IB1 FL bins, `b_bg` the same slope among IB1 background bins, and
**delta = b_fl − b_bg** is the field response specific to FL tissue. Both arms are the same
sample, section and cell type; sequencing depth enters each fit as a covariate; intervals
come from a stratified field-of-view cluster bootstrap.

```{r resp-fig}
img(file.path(IF, "figures/fig_21_interface_response.png"))
```

```{r resp-tier1}
if (!is.null(T1)) {
  for (ct in c("B","T","myeloid")) {
    d <- T1[celltype == ct & testable == TRUE][order(p_norm)][1:8]
    if (nrow(d)) print(kb(d[, .(gene, set, b_fl = round(b_fl,3), b_bg = round(b_bg,3),
        delta = round(delta,3), lo = round(ci_lo,2), hi = round(ci_hi,2),
        p_norm = signif(p_norm,3), q = signif(q_delta,3),
        mde_fold = round(mde_fold,2), conc = concordant)],
      caption = sprintf("Tier 1 (pre-declared), %s cells — top 8 by p", ct)))
  }
}
```

```{r resp-hits, results="asis"}
if (!is.null(h1)) {
  if (nrow(h1)) {
    cat('<div class="verdict-ok">\n**Genes with an FL-specific field response** — all three conditions met: BH *q* < 0.05 on the Wald p, percentile interval excluding zero, and cp10k/detection concordance.\n</div>\n')
  } else {
    cat('<div class="verdict-no">\n**No pre-declared gene shows a field response specific to FL tissue.** None of the 44 genes reaches *q* < 0.05 in B, T or myeloid cells. Read it against the detectable effects below: the FL arm is 20-22 fields of view, and the median resolvable effect is 1.09-1.14 fold, so this is a bounded null and not a demonstration that the FL is indifferent to the field.\n</div>\n')
  }
}
```

<div class="verdict-mid">
**Four genes appeared as hits in an earlier run of this analysis and they were an artifact of
the p-value, not of the defect.** *IDO1* and *CD40* in B cells and *ICOS* and *RGS13* in T
cells were reported at *q* = 0.000 before the percentile p was floored. Their percentile p
values are in fact 0.009, 0.021, 0.006 and 0.012 — nowhere near the floor — and BH over 43-44
tests puts them at *q* = 0.11, 0.22, 0.73 and 0.73. The defect adjustment barely touched them
(shifts of −0.037, +0.027, −0.017, +0.010 against deltas of 0.114, −0.155, −0.180 and
−0.042). **The attribution matters: the p-value bug removed them, and the over-fixation
covariate did not.** They are retained in the tier-1 tables as the strongest non-significant
signals, not as results.
</div>

```{r resp-hits-tbl}
if (!is.null(h2) && nrow(h2))
  kb(h2[order(celltype, -abs(delta)), .(celltype, gene,
       delta = round(delta,3), d_unadj = round(delta_unadj,3),
       fold = round(2^abs(delta),2), mde_fold = round(mde_fold,2),
       lo = round(ci_lo,2), hi = round(ci_hi,2), q_norm = signif(q_delta,3),
       p_perc = signif(p_perc,3))],
     caption = "Tier 2 genome-wide genes meeting all three conditions. Reported, NOT interpreted -- see the box below.")
```

<div class="verdict-no">
**The genome-wide tier returns `r if (is.null(h2)) NA else nrow(h2)` genes and this report
does not interpret them as biology.** Four reasons, and they compound:

1. **They sit on the detection floor.** The effects are 1.07–1.23 fold against median
   detectable effects of 1.02–1.10 fold. Nothing here is comfortably above what the design
   can resolve.
2. **There is no programme.** The list is an assortment across unrelated pathways, and
   several members (*SRSF7* splicing, *KPNA6* nuclear transport, *DHX29* helicase, *AHCYL1*)
   are housekeeping genes rather than anything the Hodgkin field would plausibly induce in
   FL tissue.
3. **One member is a contamination marker behaving inconsistently.** *CD3D* is called down in
   **B** cells, where it can only be T-cell transcript. If that were real leakage tracking
   the field, *CD3E* (delta −0.042) and *TRAC* (−0.051) would move with it. They do not, so
   *CD3D* is a single-gene fluctuation — which is what the rest of the list is likely to be.
4. **The tail calibration cannot be checked.** Tier 2 rests on the Wald p because the
   percentile p is floor-limited, and the floor is exactly what would let one verify the Wald
   approximation where it matters.

The pre-declared tier is the properly powered, hypothesis-driven test, and it is null. That
is the result of this section.
</div>

<details>
<summary>Two p-values, because a percentile bootstrap p has a floor and BH does not know it</summary>
The first version of this analysis scored the percentile p as `2*min(mean(d<=0), mean(d>=0))`,
which returns **exactly zero** when every resample falls one side of zero. BH reads zero as
infinitely significant, and the genome-wide hit list became precisely the set of genes at
that floor — **143 "hits" across three cell types, every one an artifact of the p-value
rather than a result.** Two p-values are now carried:

- **`p_perc`** — percentile, with the standard `(1 + count)/(1 + n)` correction so it can
  never be zero. Distribution-free, but floored, and under a genome-wide BH over ~6,000
  genes that floor alone gives *q* ≈ 12. **Tier 2 cannot reach *q* < 0.05 on the percentile
  p at any effect size**, which is a real resolution limit and is reported rather than
  hidden.
- **`p_norm`** — Wald on the bootstrap SD. Not floor-limited, so it can support a
  genome-wide correction, at the cost of assuming the resampling distribution is roughly
  normal.

A hit must satisfy all three of: `q_norm < 0.05`, percentile interval excluding zero, and
cp10k/detection concordance.
</details>

```{r power}
kb(PW, caption = "What a null here does and does not exclude. A |delta| smaller than med_mde_log2 could not have been resolved.")
```

# The over-fixation defect, which this step has to adjust for

<div class="verdict-mid">
**Dropping the defect cells does not leave the surviving area uniform, and that had to be
measured rather than assumed.** Defect cells are already removed **per cell** upstream of
everything here — `16_script_regions.R:166` and `16_script_celltype_pseudobulk.R:51` — which
is the method `CLAUDE.md` requires rather than the FOV-level `qc_spatial_i_fraction` flag.
So no defect transcriptome enters a bin score, a pseudobulk or a slope. But IB1 loses
**59.1%** of its cells to the defect, the defect is spatially organised as a peripheral rim,
and it does not delete cells evenly across the regions this step contrasts.
</div>

```{r defect-burden}
kb(DB, caption = "What each region lost to the per-cell defect drop")
```

<div class="verdict-no">
**Three distortions were possible and all three are present.**

1. **The two arms of the interaction are differently depleted.** FL bins carry a per-bin
   defect fraction of **`r g("fl_defect_frac", DQ)`** against background's
   **`r g("bg_defect_frac", DQ)`** — SMD **`r g("fl_vs_bg_smd", DQ)`**. Depth is a covariate
   in every fit; "how many of this bin's neighbours were deleted" was not.
2. **The exposure axis partly tracks defect burden.** Within FL tissue, defect fraction rises
   with CCL17+CCL22: bin-level rho **`r if (!is.null(DVE)) DVE[level=="bin", rho] else NA`**
   (*p* = `r if (!is.null(DVE)) signif(DVE[level=="bin", p],3) else NA`), FOV-level
   **`r g("rho_defect_exposure_fov", DQ)`** (*p* = `r g("p_defect_exposure_fov", DQ)`), with an
   SMD of **`r g("smd_defect_high_vs_low", DQ)`** across the low/high exposure split. This is
   consistent with something already on record: `qc_11_flattening_vs_chemokine.R` found the
   discarded cells to be chemokine-**enriched** (CCL17 1.20x, CCL22 1.18x). Field exposure and
   defect burden are genuinely coupled in this tissue.
3. **One of the three tissue pieces is defect-carved.** The identical single-linkage
   decomposition gives **`r g("pieces_pre", DQ)`** pieces on every occupied bin before the
   drop and **`r g("pieces_post", DQ)`** after it. The defect split IB1's lower tissue mass in
   two.
</div>

<div class="verdict-ok">
**What was done about each.** (1) and (2) are handled the same way: every slope in the
interaction carries the bin's **defect fraction** as a covariate alongside depth, and the
unadjusted estimate is reported beside it so the size of the adjustment is visible. On
synthetic data where a gene's entire apparent exposure effect *is* the confounder, the
unadjusted slope reads 1.611 and the adjusted −0.003.

(3) does not change the arrangement test, which used the largest piece under either
decomposition. It is left on the **post-drop** mask deliberately: a hotspot can only be
*called* in a bin retaining at least 40 cells, so siting null foci on pre-drop bins would
let them land where a hotspot could never have been detected. Observed pattern and null are
then conditioned on the same detectability. What the caveat costs is the piece
decomposition's status as anatomy — it is a map of where data survived, not of where tissue
is.
</div>

```{r defect-shift}
kb(DAS, caption = "How far adjusting for defect burden moved delta. A shift small against med_abs_delta means the defect was not driving the contrast.")
```

# Composition on the same axis

<div class="verdict-no">
**A count-based version of this analysis was computed first and is WITHDRAWN.** It regressed
each cell type's per-bin cell *count* on field exposure and returned steep negative
associations inside FL tissue for myeloid, fibroblast and endothelial cells. Those were the
bin's total, not its composition: inside FL tissue total assigned cells per bin falls with
exposure at Spearman **−0.34** against **−0.16** in background tissue, so every count fell
whether or not its share moved. The diagnostic that settles it is endothelium, whose
association **reverses** with the denominator — rho −0.378 on counts and +0.236 on shares. A
measure that changes sign when you change the denominator was measuring the denominator.
</div>

The replacement uses the **share** of assigned cells in the bin, and adds the bin's
over-fixation burden as a covariate alongside depth — not optional here, since the defect
deletes cells and therefore moves shares directly whenever it deletes cell types unevenly.

```{r comp-share}
kb(if (!is.null(CSH)) CSH[order(p_norm), .(celltype, fl_fovs, bg_fovs,
     b_fl = signif(b_fl,3), b_bg = signif(b_bg,3), delta = signif(delta,3),
     d_unadj = signif(delta_unadj,3), lo = signif(ci_lo,3), hi = signif(ci_hi,3),
     p_norm = signif(p_norm,3), q = signif(q_norm,3), mde = signif(mde,3), verdict)] else NULL,
   caption = "Change in each cell type's SHARE per doubling of CCL17+CCL22, depth and over-fixation burden held fixed. delta = FL slope minus background slope.")
```

<div class="verdict-no">
**Composition is null too.** No cell type's share responds to field exposure differently
inside FL tissue than in IB1 background tissue
(`r if (!is.null(CSH)) sprintf("all q >= %.2f", min(CSH$q_norm)) else "all q >= 0.46"`).
Myeloid is the strongest at delta
`r if (!is.null(CSH)) signif(CSH[celltype=="myeloid", delta],3) else NA`
(*p* = `r if (!is.null(CSH)) signif(CSH[celltype=="myeloid", p_norm],3) else NA`).

**Fibroblasts show what the corrections were worth.** Their raw Spearman was −0.609 inside FL
tissue against +0.035 in background — the largest apparent differential in the count-based
version. Adjusted, the delta is
`r if (!is.null(CSH)) signif(CSH[celltype=="fibro", delta],4) else NA`
(*p* = `r if (!is.null(CSH)) signif(CSH[celltype=="fibro", p_norm],3) else NA`). The whole
effect was total cell count plus over-fixation burden.
</div>

<div class="verdict-mid">
**This is where a positive result was most expected, which makes the null informative.** Step
16 established that most regional signal in IB1 is compositional rather than cell-state —
conditioned on cell type, the FL focus differs from background by zero genes within B or
within T. So composition was the leg with the best prior odds. It too comes back null once
the denominator and the fixation gradient are handled.
</div>

# What this step cannot support

- **A claim that the FL is indifferent to the Hodgkin field.** The FL arm is 20–22 fields of
  view against the background arm's 338–557. Where delta is null, consult `mde_log2` before
  reading it as absence.
- **A genome-wide claim on the percentile bootstrap.** Its floor forbids *q* < 0.05 over
  ~6,000 genes at any effect size. Tier 2 rests on the Wald approximation, and this report
  does not interpret its hits.
- **Any composition result on cell COUNTS.** Total cells per bin falls with exposure inside
  FL tissue; only the share-based, defect-adjusted version is interpretable.
- **Anything about distance from the Hodgkin field.** Axis A is rejected; every result here
  is on local field level, which is a measure of *exposure*, not of *distance to a source*.
  The two are not interchangeable in this tissue and that is one of the step's findings.
- **A bin-level or pooled contrast on this axis.** Field exposure and B share are collinear
  (SMD `r g("axisB_fb_a_smd")`); only the cell-type-conditioned version is interpretable.
- **Per-cell HRS identification**, which remains closed on this panel, so "the Hodgkin
  field" is throughout a chemokine readout and not a count of tumour cells.
- **Any cross-sample statement.** Nothing here involves RB1.
- **A defect-free reading of the exposure axis.** Field exposure and over-fixation burden are
  coupled within FL tissue (FOV rho `r g("rho_defect_exposure_fov", DQ)`). The covariate
  removes a linear association; it cannot remove the possibility that the deleted cells
  differed from the survivors in ways depth and burden do not capture.
- **The tissue-piece decomposition as anatomy.** It is post-defect-drop coverage
  (`r g("pieces_post", DQ)` pieces against `r g("pieces_pre", DQ)` pre-drop).
- **A clean verdict on lesion arrangement.** The two nulls bracket it and neither reaches
  significance; the over-fixation rim is confounded with both the hotspot positions and the
  distance to FL, and this section cannot separate a technical from a biological peripheral
  bias.
